idiom_name: single store + dispatched action values + pure reducer + subscription/selector reads
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: hold the application state in one object; accept changes only as action values that carry a type tag and a payload; apply them with a pure function reduce(state, action) that returns the next state (and the input unchanged for actions it does not handle) without mutating it; after each transition notify subscribers, which read the new state through selectors. Keep I/O, timers and persistence out of reducers - intercept them before or after the reducer (middleware) and let them dispatch further actions. Derive view data in selectors instead of storing it, and keep the state tree serializable so it can be logged, persisted, replayed and hydrated.
code_sketch:
store.dispatch({"type": "todos/todoAdded", "payload": todo})
# reducer: (state, action) -> nextState   (pure; same state for unhandled actions)
store.subscribe(() => render(select(store.getState())))
# effects: middleware intercepts dispatch, may dispatch further actions
pitfalls: Reducers that mutate the incoming state (or code that mutates the store's live state elsewhere) break identity-based change detection and history.
Selectors that return fresh objects on every call make subscribers re-render on every dispatch; memoize them or return stable slices.
Dispatch loops - an effect re-dispatching its own trigger, or a subscriber that dispatches - are the classic runaway bug; keep trigger conditions distinct.
Serializability is what buys logging, persistence and time travel; once functions, class instances or handles enter the tree those features degrade.

createSlice reducers that mix Immer draft mutation with a plain object return — Immer applies the return value when present, so any mutations to the draft are discarded; the two forms cannot be combined in one case.

createAsyncThunk used without async work: dispatching a follow-up action from inside the thunk instead of returning the payload and handling the transition in the reducer creates a double-dispatch and extra re-renders.
entityAdapter upsertOne/upsertMany does shallow merges — a nested object in the update overwrites the entire existing nested object, silently discarding fields not present in the update payload.

Selector memoization defeated by unstable inputs: a createSelector instance reused across components with different arguments (e.g., item IDs) has a cache size of 1 and returns the wrong cached result for the second caller; use selector factories or unique instances per component.
Store configuration that omits getDefaultMiddleware() loses redux-thunk and the dev-middleware mutation/serializability checks; always use the callback form when adding custom middleware.

Wrong move: adopting a global store before framework-local state is a problem -> most of the app becomes actions, reducers and selectors around state with a single reader, and teams report ~40% code reduction after ripping it back out -> instead keep local state local (useState/useReducer, Compose state holders, SwiftUI Observation) and lift only the slices distant components genuinely share.

Wrong move: routing every fetched server response through the store and hand-rolling loading/error/staleness flags -> the store becomes an incomplete request cache with stale badges, missed refetches and duplicated data -> instead keep server state in a dedicated cache (RTK Query, TanStack Query/SWR-style) and reserve the store for client state that needs the action/reducer audit path.

Wrong move: dispatching high-frequency continuous values (pointer position, scroll offsets, audio levels, per-frame simulation ticks) through the store -> every frame pays serialization, selector and subscriber overhead and the UI stutters -> instead keep continuous values outside the store and read them imperatively in the render loop, dispatching only discrete settled events (drag ended, value committed).
